spec: DESIGN.md — firmware: an emulator-centric answer, live declarations against packaged identities
description: Whole fixture machines in; the canonical firmware serializations (atlas/contract.py firmware_contract, identification_contract) out, asserted with exact equality. A firmware answer is about EMULATORS: each installed core states what it wants, where each file goes as an absolute path, and what is actually lying there. Two axes stay apart — need (required/optional) is what an emulator asks for, checked (verified/mismatch/unchecked/unknown) is what the machine answers, and 'we did not look' never collapses into 'we looked and cannot tell'. The load-bearing pair is firmware-core-that-declares-nothing-answers-nothing-needed against firmware-core-not-installed-is-unknown-not-nothing: the same empty list, opposite meanings, and only the installed flag plus a caveat tells them apart. Firmware blobs are stated as {md5, sha1, size} because firmware is not text and its identity is exactly what a real file would answer with.

vectors.name: firmware-core-that-declares-nothing-answers-nothing-needed
vectors.rationale: Criterion 1, the negative case. snes9x is installed and its .info carries no firmware block at all, so the honest answer is installed=true with an empty requirement list and no caveat: this core needs nothing. That is a different answer from the next vector's empty list, and the only field that tells them apart is installed.

vectors.rationale: Criterion 1, the positive case, through RetroDECK's sandbox paths: libretro_info_path points at /app/..., which a caller outside the Flatpak must resolve against the deployment before it can read anything. Each requirement states its absolute destination whether or not a file is there — the required BIOS verifies, the optional one is honestly missing and still says where it goes.

vectors.name: firmware-two-cores-one-identity-two-names
vectors.rationale: The case that decides the model. Gambatte wants gb_bios.bin, SameBoy wants dmg_boot.bin, and the packaged table carries both under one md5. The bytes are on disk under Gambatte's name, so Gambatte verifies and SameBoy is genuinely missing — a byte-identical file under the other name does not satisfy it, because SameBoy opens dmg_boot.bin and nothing else. Each emulator answers with its whole declaration set, so the Game Boy Color boot ROMs come along carrying system=gbc rather than being silently dropped. identify_firmware then answers the download flow from the same fixture: one content, both destinations, so the client can say 'copy what you already have' instead of 'download this'.

vectors.rationale: A declared subdirectory is part of the destination, not decoration: the answer carries the absolute bios/dc/dc_boot.bin. vectors.name: retrodeck-firmware-inventory-unclaimed-by-content-and-save-data-excluded
vectors.rationale: Criteria 5 and 6, and three bounds at once. scph1001.bin is claimed by nobody here, and it is recognised by its BYTES, not its name — the name is exactly what is untrustworthy about a file nothing declared. dc/spare.bin is unclaimed and unrecognised, which is a normal answer. dc/vmu_save_A1.bin does NOT appear: the save rule cards name it as Flycast's memory card, and reporting save data as firmware-anything is a category error. vectors.name: firmware-system-identifier-unknown-here-is-not-nothing-needed
vectors.rationale: The defect this design exists to prevent, and the half of it that a single caveat code used to hide. Nothing on this machine covers 'n64', so the answer is EMPTY plus 'system-unknown' — the identifier is not known here. That is a different instruction to a client than 'nobody declares firmware for it': one says check your vocabulary, the other says nothing to do. A consumer working in RomM slugs that forgets to translate to the frontend's names lands exactly here. The second caveat is load bearing too: without a frontend catalogue the emulators come from the cores' own systemname, so the identifier is an atlas slug and the answer says so.

vectors.name: firmware-system-filed-by-the-core-name-says-so
vectors.rationale: Only the per-file rule knows which machine a dump belongs to. mGBA serves three systems by its own database field but states one systemname, and gba_bios.bin carries no per-file rule — so its system was derived from what the whole core is called and may be wrong. The caveat names exactly which files went that way; gb_bios.bin does not appear in it, because a rule covered it. Visible beats silent: the table is deliberately not completed by hand, so the gap is reported instead.

vectors.name: firmware-a-path-that-cannot-be-looked-at-is-not-an-absent-file
vectors.rationale: Four path kinds, four answers. The declared destination cannot be read at all, so present is null — 'could not look' is not 'not there' — checked stays null, satisfied is undecided, and requirements_met refuses to be true. A directory sitting where a file belongs is the fourth kind: no file is there, and none can be placed there either, which only the caveat says.

vectors.name: firmware-a-declared-path-never-leaves-the-firmware-root
vectors.rationale: firmwareN_path is relative by contract, but it comes out of an editable config and every read atlas then does is derived from it — presence, size, digest, and the directories the unclaimed scan walks. A declaration that climbs out of the root is refused and stated, so the scan cannot be steered at files outside the firmware tree. The core's other, well-formed declaration is answered normally: this is a refusal, not a dropped core.

vectors.name: firmware-a-symlinked-declaration-does-not-escape-the-root
vectors.rationale: A lexical check is not a boundary. 'etclink/hostname' stays under the firmware root on paper while etclink is a symlink to /etc, so the declared path and the root are both resolved through the seam before they are compared. The declaration is refused, it stays visible on the core as a refusal rather than vanishing, requirements_met is null because a required file was never looked at, and the unclaimed scan never gains /etc as a directory: only ps1.bin, a real file in the root, comes back.

vectors.name: firmware-dotdot-is-applied-where-the-symlink-landed
vectors.rationale: Resolution order, and it is not a preference: the kernel resolves a component and then walks up from where it landed, so 'pcsx2/bios/../scph5501.bin' with pcsx2/bios linked to the firmware root means <root>/../scph5501.bin — outside. Collapsing '..' lexically first would eat the symlink before anything looked at it and answer <root>/pcsx2/scph5501.bin, verifying a file the core will never open. The kernel opens the file, so the declaration is refused, the refusal names the reason, and requirements_met stays out of true.

Equality is inside, not outside — an earlier revision refused it and broke a stock installation. A symlink loop is not a path leaving the firmware root — a consumer branching on firmware-path-escapes-root would act on something that did not happen. The refusal carries its own code, and refused records which fact it rests on.
